subject: music
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Music and words; music for dance
Music for small ensemble, stage and screen

questions.q: Which period is generally dated approximately 1600-1750?
questions.explain: The Baroque period runs roughly from 1600 to 1750, ending around the death of J. S. Bach.

questions.q: In Baroque music, the basso continuo is typically played by which combination of instruments?
options: A keyboard (e.g. harpsichord) plus a bass instrument such as cello
A full string orchestra without keyboard
questions.explain: The continuo combines a chordal keyboard instrument, usually harpsichord, with a sustaining bass line instrument such as cello or bassoon.

questions.q: Sudden shifts between loud and soft with little gradual change, known as terraced dynamics, are most characteristic of which period?
questions.explain: Terraced dynamics, contrasting loud and soft in blocks, are typical of Baroque style and instruments such as the harpsichord.

questions.q: Vivaldi's 'The Four Seasons' is an example of which genre?
questions.explain: 'The Four Seasons' is a set of solo violin concertos, each accompanied by a string orchestra and continuo.

questions.q: Which three main sections make up sonata form?
questions.explain: Sonata form presents themes in the exposition, transforms them in the development and restates them in the recapitulation.

questions.q: Which of these composers belongs to the Classical period?
questions.explain: Mozart is a central Classical-period composer; Bach and Vivaldi are Baroque and Tchaikovsky is Romantic.

questions.q: A broken-chord left-hand accompaniment pattern known as the Alberti bass is most associated with which period?
questions.explain: The Alberti bass, a broken-chord accompaniment, is a hallmark of Classical keyboard textures.

questions.q: You hear a work in which a single virtuoso violinist alternates and contrasts with a full orchestra across three movements (fast-slow-fast). What is it most likely to be?
questions.explain: Contrast between a soloist and orchestra across a fast-slow-fast three-movement plan defines the solo concerto.

questions.q: What is the term for singing many notes to a single syllable of text?
questions.explain: A melisma is a run of several notes sung on one syllable, contrasting with syllabic word-setting.

questions.q: When the music imitates the meaning of the words, for example rising pitch on the word 'ascend', this is called:
questions.explain: Word painting (text painting) uses musical gestures to reflect the literal meaning of the lyrics.

questions.q: The minuet is a stately dance normally written in which metre?
questions.explain: The minuet is an elegant dance in triple time, usually notated in 3/4.

questions.q: A song is described as 'strophic'. What does this mean?
options: The same music is repeated for each verse of the text
New music is written continuously throughout
It has no words, only vocalisation
It is sung by a full choir in harmony
questions.explain: In a strophic song each verse uses the same melody, as opposed to through-composed settings.

questions.q: A German solo song for voice and piano, such as those by Schubert, is known as a:
questions.explain: The Lied is a German art song for solo voice and piano, strongly associated with Schubert.

questions.q: You hear an elegant 19th-century ballroom dance in a swaying triple time with a strong first beat. Which dance is this most likely to be?
questions.explain: The waltz is a 19th-century ballroom dance in triple time with an emphasised first beat and swaying feel.

questions.q: A string quartet is made up of which four instruments?
options: Violin, viola, cello and double bass
questions.explain: The standard string quartet comprises first violin, second violin, viola and cello.

questions.q: In opera and film music, a leitmotif is best described as:
options: A recurring musical theme linked to a character or idea
questions.explain: A leitmotif is a short recurring theme associated with a particular character, place or idea.

questions.q: A standard piano trio consists of which instruments?
questions.explain: The classic piano trio combines piano with violin and cello.

questions.q: In a film, the same short tune plays every time a particular hero appears on screen. This use of music is an example of:
questions.explain: A theme that recurs to signal a specific character is functioning as a leitmotif.

questions.q: In Indian classical music, the melodic framework on which a performance is based is called the:
questions.explain: A raga is the set of notes and melodic conventions that shape an Indian classical performance.

questions.q: A gamelan ensemble, built largely from tuned metallophones and gongs, originates from which region?
questions.explain: The gamelan is an Indonesian percussion ensemble, particularly associated with Java and Bali.

questions.q: In Indian classical music, the repeating rhythmic cycle played on the tabla is known as the:
questions.explain: The tala is the cyclic rhythmic framework of Indian classical music, commonly realised on the tabla.

questions.q: You hear a West African drumming piece in which a lead drummer plays a phrase that the group answers, over interlocking layered rhythms. Which two features are these?
questions.explain: African drumming characteristically combines call and response between leader and group with layered polyrhythms.
